John Scory
jon skor'e
n. (John Scory, d. 1585, Marian exile and superintendent of the English congregation at Emden, afterwards Bishop of Hereford)
Hebrew Yochanan through Latin Johannes, the LORD is gracious; Scory, an English surname of uncertain origin.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

John Scory had been a Dominican friar before the Reformation reached him, was made Bishop of Rochester and then of Chichester under Edward VI, and was deprived by Mary. He crossed to Emden in East Friesland, where a sizeable English colony had gathered, and acted as superintendent of their congregation, writing pastoral letters of comfort back to the faithful in England and seeing some translation work through the Emden presses. At Elizabeth's accession he returned and was given Hereford, a border diocese he held for twenty-six years. The dictionary records him with the honesty the record requires: a man who came the whole distance from the cloister to a Reformed pulpit, who in exile wrote to encourage prisoners he could not reach, and whose long tenure at Hereford drew complaints about his management of the see's property. Both things are true and the entry keeps both. Scory's letters to the persecuted belong with the best of that literature; the later complaints are a reminder that the Reformation's recovered gospel did not instantly reform every man who preached it.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines superintendent as one who has the oversight and charge of something, and comfort as to strengthen and console.

expand to see more

SUPERINTEND'ENT, n. One who has the oversight and charge of some place, person or business, with the power of direction.

COM'FORT, v.t. To strengthen; to invigorate; to console or cheer in affliction.

FRI'AR, n. An appellation common to monks of all orders; a brother of a religious order.

EPIS'TLE, n. A writing communicated from one person to another; a letter.

Key Scripture

2Co 1:4 — "Who comforteth us in all our tribulation, that we may be able to comfort them which are in any trouble, by the comfort wherewith we ourselves are comforted of God."

Heb 10:34 — "For ye had compassion of me in my bonds, and took joyfully the spoiling of your goods, knowing in yourselves that ye have in heaven a better and an enduring substance."

Phi 1:7 — "Even as it is meet for me to think this of you all, because I have you in my heart; inasmuch as both in my bonds, and in the defence and confirmation of the gospel, ye all are partakers of my grace."

Col 4:18 — "The salutation by the hand of me Paul. Remember my bonds. Grace be with you. Amen."

Modern Corruption

A former friar turned Reformed bishop who wrote letters of comfort to the persecuted from exile at Emden.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the modern wish for unmixed subjects — either the heroic exile or the grasping prelate, and never the same man. Scory wrote to strangers in prison and he also quarrelled over the revenues of Hereford, and the dictionary names both because Scripture never flatters its own servants.

The principle to recover is that comfort is a ministry and not a mood, and that the comfort God gives is given in order to be handed on. He “comforteth us in all our tribulation, that we may be able to comfort them which are in any trouble” (2Co 1:4). The Hebrews had done it in the flesh: they “took joyfully the spoiling of your goods” (Heb 10:34) for the sake of brethren in bonds. And Paul's shortest request, written in his own hand, is the whole of what an exile can send home — “Remember my bonds” (Col 4:18).

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek parakaleo (G3870), to call alongside, to comfort; Greek paraklesis (G3874), consolation.

expand to see more

Greek parakaleo (G3870) — to call to one's side, to comfort, to exhort; 2 Corinthians 1:4.

Greek paraklesis (G3874) — consolation, comfort, encouragement; 2 Corinthians 1:4.

Greek thlipsis (G2347) — tribulation, pressure, affliction; 2 Corinthians 1:4.

Greek harpage (G724) — plundering, spoiling of goods; Hebrews 10:34.

Greek desmos (G1199) — a bond, imprisonment; Colossians 4:18.

Usage

"“that we may be able to comfort them which are in any trouble” (2Co 1:4) — letters from Emden to Marian prisoners."

"“took joyfully the spoiling of your goods” (Heb 10:34) — a deprived bishop writing to the deprived."

"“Remember my bonds” (Col 4:18) — twenty-six later years at Hereford, complaints and all."
